title: The Last Protocol Again
premise: Wendell Sandoval, the colony of Meridian's aging xenolinguist, has spent thirty years maintaining a beacon whose original purpose was erased from every archive. When the colony's children begin dreaming in a language only Wendell recognizes—the tongue of the Vessh, the alien species official history says never lived here—he realizes the beacon is a memorial transmitter, and that someone rewrote reality to hide a massacre. As he decodes the children's shared dream, he uncovers proof buried in his own suppressed memories: he helped broadcast the cover-up in exchange for the colonists' survival. In the end, Wendell must choose between reactivating the beacon and exposing the truth—which will sever Meridian from its protective patron—or letting the lie stand, and he chooses truth, transmitting the massacre to the stars as the children, finally fluent, sing the names of the dead.
about_author: Ulyana Ravensworth is the pen name of a former field interpreter who spent a decade documenting endangered languages before turning to fiction. She writes from a coastal town where she keeps an amateur radio license and a stubborn belief that every silenced voice eventually finds a frequency.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He performs his solitary maintenance ritual on the ridge-top beacon, speaking aloud in dead languages because he no longer dreams in any living one. A child, Ilsa, watches him and repeats a phrase she shouldn't know. Emotional beat: quiet loneliness cracked open by the first impossible word.

chapters.title: Shared Sleep
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Seven children across Meridian wake having dreamed the same dream: a red plain, towers falling, a voice counting names. Their parents dismiss it as a fad; their drawings match too precisely. Emotional beat: eerie wonder curdling into fear as the adults close ranks.

chapters.title: Records of Nothing
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He searches the colonial archives for the Vessh and finds pristine records proving they never existed—too pristine, with metadata timestamps all identical. His own service file contains a fourteen-month gap. Emotional beat: scholarly curiosity hardening into dread.

chapters.title: The Language Under the Skin
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He transcribes the children's dream-phrases and confirms they are Vessh—not learned but remembered, grammatically perfect in ways no teaching could produce. The beacon's transmission logs show it has been broadcasting a counter-signal for decades. Emotional beat: vertigo as his expertise becomes an accusation.

chapters.title: What the Patron Gave
chapters.summary: Administrator Cho's POV. Cho knows what Wendell is finding. Flashbacks reveal the bargain: the Vessh were exterminated by Meridian's patron consortium after first contact failed, and the survivors' silence was purchased with terraforming, medicine, and edited memory implants. Emotional beat: guilt wearing the mask of duty.

chapters.title: The Gap in Wendell
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Hypnosis-adjacent memory work with Ilsa's grandmother surfaces his missing months: Wendell himself recorded the denial broadcast, believing refusal meant the colony's air supply would be cut. He understands why he can't dream in human languages—he gave them away. Emotional beat: self-loathing and grief entwined.

chapters.title: Counter-Signal
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The children's dreams intensify into full waking visions; the beacon begins responding to their speech, and Ilsa realizes it isn't a machine but a repository—a Vessh mind-archive that has been waiting for fluent speakers. Emotional beat: terror transforming into fierce belonging.

chapters.title: The Choice They Made For Us
chapters.summary: Cho's POV. Cho confronts Wendell on the ridge, offering him erasure again: forget, and Meridian keeps its patron's protection. Wendell refuses. Cho orders the beacon jammed and Wendell detained, but half the colony's children walk out of school and stand silent at the fence. Emotional beat: the machinery of survival meeting the cost of complicity.

chapters.title: Names of the Dead
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, climax. With the children chanting the archived names, Wendell overrides the jamming using the maintenance backdoor he built himself over thirty invisible years. The beacon broadcasts the massacre in Vessh and human tongues simultaneously, unalterable, aimed at every listening world. Emotional beat: catharsis—grief finally spoken at full volume.

chapters.title: After the Signal
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV, resolution. The patron cuts supply lines; the colony endures a hard year but holds together, poorer and honest. The children keep the language alive; Wendell, dying slowly, teaches until he can't, then dreams—in Vessh—for the first time. Emotional beat: mourning resolved into inheritance and belonging.
